title: Median of Every Window
statement:
You get an integer array nums and a window size k. A window of k consecutive elements starts at index 0 and slides right one step at a time until it touches the last element.

Return the median of every window, in order. The median of a window is its middle value after sorting. When k is even there are two middle values, and the median is their average, which may end in .5. Answers within 10⁻⁵ are accepted.

examples.why: Sorted windows: [1, 4, 7], [1, 3, 7], [3, 7, 8], [2, 3, 8]. Take the middle of each.
With an even window, average the two middle values: (2 + 5) / 2, (2 + 8) / 2, (1 + 8) / 2.
Adding the two values overflows a 32-bit integer. Average them in a wider type, or as a / 2 + b / 2.

hints: Sorting every window costs O(k log k) per step. What do you actually need from a window to read its median?
Only the boundary between the lower half and the upper half matters. Keep the lower half in a max-heap and the upper half in a min-heap; the median sits on their tops.
Heaps cannot delete an arbitrary value cheaply. Leave the outgoing value inside, count it as gone, and throw it away only when it reaches the top of its heap.

explain.intuition:
This is the running-median trick with one extra problem: values also leave. Split the window into a lower half in a max-heap and an upper half in a min-heap, with the lower half holding the extra element when k is odd. Then the median is the top of the lower heap, or the average of both tops.

Adding is easy: push to the correct side and rebalance. Removing is the hard part, because a heap only gives you its top. The fix is lazy deletion: when a value leaves the window, keep it in the heap but stop counting it in that side's size. Whenever a stale value surfaces at the top of a heap, pop it then. Stale values below the top do no harm, because only the tops are ever read.
steps: Keep a max-heap lo and a min-heap hi, each with a count of its live elements. Store (value, index) so every element is unique and stale entries are easy to spot by index.
For each new index i: if i ≥ k, the element at i − k leaves. Decide which side it is on by comparing with the top of lo, and decrement that side's count.

Push the new element into lo, clean stale entries off its top, and move that top to hi. Whatever the new value is, the largest live value of the lower side ends up in the upper side, so the split stays correct.
Rebalance so that lo has as many live elements as hi, or one more, moving tops across and cleaning stale tops as you go.
Once i ≥ k − 1, record the median from the cleaned tops.
pitfalls: Comparing heap sizes including stale entries. Balance must use the live counts, or the median drifts.
Reading a heap top without first popping stale entries, which can return a value that already left the window.
Averaging two large values with 32-bit math; the third example overflows.

complexity.space: O(n) in the worst case, since stale entries can pile up

solutions.title: Sort every window
solutions.idea: Copy each window, sort it, and read the middle.

solutions.title: Two heaps with lazy deletion
solutions.idea: Lower half in a max-heap, upper half in a min-heap. Outgoing elements are only counted out, and popped once they reach a top.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def windowMedians(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> List[float]:
        lo, hi = [], []          # lo: max-heap of (-value, -index); hi: min-heap of (value, index)
        lo_live = hi_live = 0
        start = 0                # indexes below start have left the window

        def clean():
            while lo and -lo[0][1] < start:
                heapq.heappop(lo)
            while hi and hi[0][1] < start:
                heapq.heappop(hi)

        out = []
        for i, x in enumerate(nums):
            if i >= k:
                gone = i - k
                clean()
                if (nums[gone], gone) <= (-lo[0][0], -lo[0][1]):
                    lo_live -= 1
                else:
                    hi_live -= 1
                start = gone + 1
            # enter through lo, then pass lo's largest live value up to hi
            heapq.heappush(lo, (-x, -i))
            clean()
            v, j = heapq.heappop(lo)
            heapq.heappush(hi, (-v, -j))
            hi_live += 1
            while lo_live > hi_live + 1:
                clean()
                v, j = heapq.heappop(lo)
                heapq.heappush(hi, (-v, -j))
                lo_live -= 1
                hi_live += 1
            while lo_live < hi_live:
                clean()
                v, j = heapq.heappop(hi)
                heapq.heappush(lo, (-v, -j))
                hi_live -= 1
                lo_live += 1
            if i >= k - 1:
                clean()
                out.append(-lo[0][0] if k % 2 else (-lo[0][0] + hi[0][0]) / 2)
        return out

followups: With a sorted container that supports O(log k) insert and delete by value, the code gets much shorter. What would you use in each language?
Return the k-th smallest value of every window instead of the median. Which part of the two-heap idea changes?
